title: Databricks Pricing: DBU Rates and Costs (2026 Guide)
summary: Databricks pricing works per DBU (Databricks Unit), not per fixed plan, so you can estimate monthly costs based on compute usage and workload.
body_markdown:
## Hidden Costs and Limits That Change the Bill


Whichever way the compute-type question falls, the per-DBU rate covers only part of what you pay, and other units on other invoices cover the rest.


A DBU is the unit Databricks meters for processing; the VM hours, gigabytes moved, gigabytes stored and support percentage around it come on separate bills.


Below, the chart sorts those omissions by where they show up:


- The Databricks invoice
- The cloud provider's invoice
- Neither until you hit a wall


Read it as a checklist of line items to estimate before you compare any two list prices. A line you leave out of one vendor's quote but keep in another's makes the comparison meaningless.


*(chart placement)*


### Cloud charges billed outside Databricks


On classic compute, the DBU rate pays for the Databricks software only. Your cloud provider bills the virtual machines that run your cluster, per instance-hour, on a separate invoice.


So the Databricks line can look modest while the VM line beside it is as large or larger, and anyone who reads only the rate card sees a fraction of the total.


Move on to storage and network and the pattern repeats. Your data sits in your own cloud storage account, billed by the gigabyte stored and by requests.


If data leaves a region or a cloud, to a BI tool or another team's account, the provider bills egress per gigabyte. If your pipeline reads across regions, that transfer cost recurs on every run.


On serverless, one bill replaces two, because the VM cost is folded into the DBU price. It doesn't remove your storage or egress charges.


### Idle compute and autoscaling surprises


Metered for as long as they're running, not for as long as they're working: that is how classic clusters bill. A cluster waiting for the next job, or held open by an interactive notebook someone forgot, accrues both DBUs and VM hours.


> Metered for as long as they're running, not for as long as they're working: that is how classic clusters bill.


You can cap that waste with auto-termination, but only if it's set, and a short setting trades savings for slower restarts.


Then there is autoscaling, a second variable. A cluster that scales up for one heavy stage and scales down slowly keeps paying for workers it no longer needs. Many tiny jobs hit a minimum far more often than a few long ones.


**When work stops, serverless stops billing** , but it can carry its own minimums and startup behavior, so check the documented floor for each serverless product against how short your jobs are.


### Features and limits that depend on tier or compute type


Not every feature is available on every plan or compute type. Some governance, security and networking capabilities are gated to higher tiers, and some features run only on serverless or only on classic.


If a requirement such as network isolation or fine-grained access control is mandatory for you, price the tier that includes it, not the cheapest one.


Budget for support too, since paid support plans are typically a share of spend or a set fee, so they scale with your bill.


Finally, quotas and concurrency limits cap how many clusters, jobs or SQL queries run at once. Hitting one doesn't raise the bill; it queues your work or forces a quota request.


That delay is a cost your estimate should include before you commit to a term.
